issues.item: Triggers: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
issues.explanation: For a police trauma profile, the trigger set is not clinically coherent as a group. Physical touch can fit, but crash imagery and burnt smell together suggest a road traffic accident or fire-related trauma rather than police-related trauma, and there is no supporting memory or appraisal content tying these cues back to police trauma.

issues.item: Triggers: Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
issues.explanation: The contamination appraisal is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. It more commonly fits sexual assault or severe physical violation. Here it is unsupported by the trigger and memory items, which focus on fragmented recall and guilt rather than shame/violation themes.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: Hypervigilance towards dangerous people could occur after police trauma, but in this profile it is weakly supported because the triggers point toward accident/fire cues rather than interpersonal threat cues. This creates a cross-node mismatch between maladaptive strategy content and the rest of the selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: 'Contamination/feeling dirty' is more typically coherent with sexual assault or severe bodily violation trauma. In a police-trauma profile, it is hard to reconcile this appraisal unless there are other items indicating sexualized assault, humiliating bodily violation, or related memory content, which are absent here.

A tactile trigger of general physical touch would usually imply trauma involving bodily contact/restraint. That could occur in police trauma, but in this profile there is no supporting memory or appraisal content about physical restraint, assault, or contact-based threat. Given the rest of the profile emphasizes authority/police cues, danger, mistrust, and guilt, this broad touch trigger stands out as insufficiently supported and clinically hard to place.

vignette:
Ravi is a 41-year-old graphic designer living in a quiet suburb outside Chicago with his wife and two children. The event that changed everything happened eighteen months ago, during what should have been a routine evening. He had been driving home from a late client meeting when a patrol car pulled him over for a broken taillight. What began as a minor traffic stop escalated within seconds. The officer, a large man with a close-cropped beard, ordered Ravi out of the car so abruptly that he stumbled. Before he could explain, he was on the ground, his face pressed against the cold asphalt, a knee grinding into his lower back. He heard the officer shouting something about reaching for something, though Ravi's hands had never left the steering wheel. In the chaos, he smelled the officer's sweat mixed with the acrid burn of exhaust from the patrol car idling nearby. That burnt smell, metallic and sharp, is now seared into his memory. When he encounters it-a neighbor lighting a grill, a passing diesel truck-his chest tightens and the scene floods back: the weight on his spine, the gravel biting his cheek, the helplessness. The memory itself is fragmented; Ravi knows what happened, but when his wife asks him to describe it, the words dissolve. He starts a sentence, loses the thread, and falls silent, unable to explain the sequence or why it felt so wrong. What he can articulate, with a hollow certainty, is that he was betrayed. The officer had smiled at him as he handed back his license moments before the stop turned violent. That smile, that trust, now feels like a trap.

In the months that followed, Ravi's view of the world hardened. He had always been cautious, but now he scans every parking lot for uniforms, for the silhouette of a patrol car, for any figure in authority. He is certain that people-especially those in positions of power-cannot be trusted. The world, he has come to believe, is a dangerous place where safety is an illusion. This belief feeds directly into his hypervigilance. Every man in a uniform becomes a potential threat, and that threat triggers the memory again: the knee, the smell, the shame. The cycle tightens. Because the world feels so unsafe, Ravi has begun rehearsing conversations before any interaction, even trivial ones. Before ordering coffee, he runs through every possible question the barista might ask, every response he might give. He tells himself this will prevent another misunderstanding, another escalation. But the rehearsals only reinforce his sense of danger. Each time he mentally prepares, he is reminded that the world requires constant defense, that betrayal is always waiting. The rehearsals also make the memory more vivid. As he practices what to say, his mind supplies the officer's voice, the cold ground, the smell of burnt exhaust, and he feels the guilt wash over him-guilt that he didn't say the right thing, that he must have done something to provoke the stop. He has stopped making any plans for the future. When his wife suggests a weekend trip, he feels a wave of dread. Planning implies hope, and hope feels naive. Instead, he stays home, vigilant for dangerous people in his own neighborhood, watching from the window as neighbors walk their dogs.

His avoidance has cost him. At work, he used to lead client pitches; now he delegates them, avoiding the eye contact and small talk that feel like invitations to conflict. His boss has noticed his withdrawal. Ravi's rehearsed scripts keep interactions flat, and his colleagues sense a distance they cannot name. He finally sought help after his wife found him standing at the kitchen window at 2 a.m., staring at a parked car that resembled an unmarked police cruiser. When she touched his shoulder, he flinched. What frightens him most is not the memory itself, but the certainty that it will happen again-that no amount of rehearsal, no amount of watching, can keep him safe. He is exhausted, and he is hoping that talking about it might finally break the loop.
